questions.passage: Readers of this chapter may expect a verdict on whether the amnesty worked. They will not find one. The records that would settle it—who returned, and when, and whether they were prosecuted—were compiled by the very ministry the amnesty was designed to protect, and that ministry had every reason to make the numbers come out well. What can be shown, and what the following pages attempt, is how thoroughly that interest shaped the archive on which every later assessment, favorable and hostile alike, has unknowingly depended.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To show that the archive underlying every later assessment of the amnesty was shaped by the interests of the body that compiled it.
To demonstrate, on the basis of the ministry's own records, that the amnesty achieved its stated aims.
To compare the favorable and the hostile assessments of the amnesty that scholars have offered.
To recommend that historians abandon the study of the amnesty altogether.

questions.passage: It is usually said that the moth is drawn to the flame. The phrasing smuggles in a theory. Moths navigate by holding a fixed angle to a distant light—the moon—which, being effectively infinitely far away, keeps the angle constant and the flight straight. A candle is not infinitely far, so holding that same angle to it produces not a straight line but a spiral, tightening inward. The moth is not attracted to the flame at all; it is doing exactly what has always carried it straight, in the presence of an object its method was never built for.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It questions the assumption buried in a familiar description, explains the mechanism that description misreads, and then restates what is actually happening.
It describes an insect's behavior, surveys several competing explanations, and endorses the oldest of them.
It presents a natural phenomenon and argues that it remains entirely unexplained.
It traces the history of how the navigation of moths came to be discovered.

questions.passage: The usual defense of the jury is that twelve ordinary people bring the community's common sense to bear on the evidence. Its most interesting justification, though, is nearly the opposite: that the jury's inexperience is the point, since a body that will never try another case cannot develop the quiet cynicism—the settled sense of what defendants of this kind are usually like—that afflicts every professional who does the work daily. Amateurism, on this account, is not a defect the system tolerates but the safeguard it is built around.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It restates the usual defense given in the first sentence in more precise terms.
It raises an objection to the jury system that the final sentence goes on to concede.
It offers evidence that professional judges reach better verdicts than juries do.
It advances a second, contrasting justification for the institution, which the final sentence then generalizes into a claim about the institution's design.

questions.passage: He wrote the letter of acceptance that night, and read it over, and did not seal it. In the morning he wrote another, declining, and read that one over too, and did not seal it either. For a week both letters lay in the drawer, and he found that he took a certain pleasure in opening it—not to choose, but to look at them lying there, each one a life he still had, and would have only so long as he did not decide.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Havel cannot decide because he lacks sufficient information about the post he has been offered.
Havel has secretly resolved to decline the post but is unable to admit it to himself.
Havel prolongs the decision because remaining undecided lets him keep both futures, either of which choosing would end.
Havel resents having been offered a choice that he never sought in the first place.

questions.passage: The mimic octopus does not merely change color; it changes creature. Confronted by one predator it flattens its arms and undulates as a poisonous flatfish; threatened by another, it withdraws six arms into a burrow and splays the remaining two in the banded pattern of a sea snake. What is unusual is the selectivity: the impersonation is matched to the audience. The sea-snake display appears almost exclusively when the attacker is a damselfish—an animal that is itself hunted by sea snakes.
questions.question: According to the text, what determines which impersonation the mimic octopus performs?
options: The color and texture of the surrounding seafloor where the octopus is hiding.
The number of arms that the octopus is able to withdraw into its burrow.
The identity of the animal threatening it, so that the display is matched to what that particular attacker fears.
The time of day at which the encounter with the predator happens to occur.

questions.passage: The historian Béla Marek is known for letting a single mundane document overturn a grand narrative without ever announcing that it has. A reader illustrating this method might quote the passage in which ______
questions.question: Which quotation from Marek's writing most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “The chronicles' account of the siege is, as I shall argue at length in the following chapter, entirely without foundation.”

“The garrison's bread ledger for that October records the same four hundred rations issued daily, without interruption, through the very week the chronicles describe the town as starving under siege.”
“The garrison's bread ledger for that October survives in the municipal archive, and is in remarkably good condition.”
“No historian has yet troubled to explain why the chronicles describe the town as starving at all.”

questions.passage: A team reported that patients given a room with a window overlooking trees recovered from surgery faster than patients in windowless rooms, and concluded that a view of nature speeds recovery.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the team's conclusion?

The trees outside the windows lost their leaves during part of the study period.
A later study found a similar effect at a hospital in a different country.
The rooms with tree views all lay on the ward's quiet eastern side, while the windowless rooms adjoined the service lifts and were markedly noisier at all hours.

questions.passage: Researchers trained crows to drop stones into a tube of water to raise a floating treat within reach; the birds soon came to prefer sinking objects over floating ones and solid objects over hollow ones. To test whether they grasped displacement itself, the team then offered a wide tube and a narrow one, each holding the same treat at the same height. A stone dropped into the narrow tube raises the level far more than the same stone does in the wide one, and the crows, given a free choice, went to the narrow tube first on the great majority of trials—but only when the tubes were transparent. When the tubes were made opaque, their choices fell to chance. The results suggest that the crows' success depends on ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: a general preference for narrow openings that the birds display regardless of what the tubes contain.
monitoring the visible level of the water rather than on any grasp of how a stone's size relates to the volume it displaces.
their memory of which of the two tubes had contained a treat on previous trials.
the weight of the stones they are handed rather than the volume those stones occupy.

questions.passage: A city began requiring landlords to state, in every listing, the building's average heating cost for the previous winter. Within a year, rents for the most poorly insulated apartments had fallen 9%, while rents for well-insulated units were unchanged. Landlords' own costs did not change over the period, and no unit was renovated. The pattern suggests that, before the law, tenants of the poorly insulated apartments had been ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: agreeing to rents that did not reflect a heating cost they had no way of anticipating.
systematically overcharged by landlords who knew that those units were well insulated.
refusing to rent any apartment whose heating costs were unusually high.
renovating their own apartments in order to bring their heating bills down.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Two tunnels were bored through the same mountain range.
  • Tunnel J used a tunnel boring machine; it advanced 21 meters per day and cost $840 million.
  • Tunnel K used drill-and-blast; it advanced 6 meters per day and cost $610 million.
  • Both tunnels are 14 km long.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the difference in how quickly the two tunnels advanced. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Tunnel J used a tunnel boring machine, whereas Tunnel K used the drill-and-blast method.
Tunnel K cost $610 million and advanced 6 meters per day through the mountain range.
Though both tunnels run 14 km through the same range, Tunnel J's boring machine advanced 21 meters a day—three and a half times the 6 meters a day that drill-and-blast managed at Tunnel K.
Both of the tunnels are 14 km long and pass through the same mountain range.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • “Ghost fishing” is what happens when lost or discarded fishing gear goes on catching animals.
  • A lost gill net can drift for years.
  • It continues to trap fish, which die and attract scavengers.
  • The scavengers are trapped in turn, and the cycle repeats.
  • Modern nets are made of nylon, which does not rot.
questions.question: The student wants to explain ghost fishing to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Modern fishing nets are made of nylon, a material that does not rot away in seawater.
A gill net that has been lost or discarded can drift in the ocean for years.
Ghost fishing occurs when lost fishing gear continues to catch animals.

Ghost fishing is what happens when lost or discarded gear goes on catching animals by itself—a drifting nylon net, which never rots, traps fish that die and draw scavengers, which are trapped in turn, and the cycle repeats for years.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The researcher Cato Merz hypothesized that, among island bird species, those living where there are fewer predators tend to have weaker flight muscles.
  • Species D: its island has 9 predator species; flight-muscle index 88.
  • Species E: its island has 0 predator species; flight-muscle index 21.
  • Species F: its island has 4 predator species; flight-muscle index 54.
questions.question: The student wants to use the data to support Merz's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The species on the island with no predators, E, had by far the weakest flight muscles (index 21), while the species on the island with the most predators, D (9 species), had the strongest (88).
Species F lives on an island with 4 predator species and has a flight-muscle index of 54.
All three of the species are birds that live on islands.
Species D has a higher flight-muscle index than both Species E and Species F.

questions.passage: The reader who comes to this book for a portrait of the composer will be disappointed, and deliberately so. We have portraits enough, and they are all the same portrait: the deaf titan shaking his fist at fate. What we do not have is any account of the four copyists, the two publishers, and the dozen patrons without whose ordinary, uncelebrated labor not one bar of that music would ever have reached a page. This is a book about them, and the composer appears in it only where they touched him.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To offer a fuller and more accurate portrait of the composer than earlier biographies have managed.
To argue that the composer's reputation as a titan is entirely undeserved.
To shift attention away from the composer himself and onto the uncelebrated people whose labor made his music available.
To catalogue the technical errors that copyists introduced into the composer's scores.

questions.passage: Ask why the piece hangs in the museum and you will be told it is a masterpiece. Ask how it came to be judged one and the answer turns circular: it hangs in the museum. The judgment and the placement each rest on the other. The record, though, shows the placement came first—acquired cheaply, in a lot, by a curator who wanted the frame. What we now experience as the painting's self-evident quality is, in part, the residue of a century of being looked at in a room reserved for quality.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It defines a term, offers two examples of it, and then proposes a test for identifying it.
It presents two rival theories of artistic value and declines to choose between them.
It narrates the acquisition of a painting and traces the rise of its market price.
It exposes a circularity in a common justification, notes historical evidence that breaks the circle, and then reinterprets the phenomenon in light of it.

questions.passage: Every account of the famine begins with the failed harvest of 1846. The harvest of 1846 failed across the whole of northern Europe, and in most of it nobody starved; what distinguished the districts where people died was not the weather but who was entitled to the grain that those districts went on exporting throughout the famine. A crop failure is a fact about rainfall. A famine is a fact about law.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It supplies meteorological detail explaining why the harvest of 1846 failed so widely.
It concedes that the failed harvest was, after all, the decisive cause of the famine.
It undercuts the starting point common to existing accounts by identifying a factor those accounts omit, a distinction the final two sentences then compress.
It introduces an objection that the final two sentences go on to refute.

questions.passage: The nephews arrived on Thursday and were very kind to her. They asked her where things were kept, and she told them; and where the deeds were, and she told them that too; and by Saturday there was nothing left in the house that they needed her to explain. She had supposed, all those years, that she was indispensable, and she had been right—but she saw now that being indispensable lasts exactly as long as no one has troubled to ask you how it is done.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Sabine is grieving the loss of an employer to whom she had been devoted for many years.
Sabine realizes that her indispensability rested only on knowledge no one had asked her for, and that it dissolved the moment they did.
Sabine resents the nephews for the condescending kindness with which they treat her.
Sabine had long understood that her position in the household was an insecure one.

questions.passage: The Greenland shark grows about one centimeter a year and does not reproduce until it is roughly 150 years old. Radiocarbon dating of the lenses of its eyes—tissue that forms before birth and is never afterward replaced—has put the oldest individuals at nearly four centuries. The method works precisely because the lens is inert: unlike muscle or skin, which are constantly rebuilt out of whatever the animal has lately eaten, the lens preserves the chemistry of the year the shark was born.
questions.question: According to the text, why can the lens of the eye be used to determine a Greenland shark's age?
options: It grows at a steady rate of about one centimeter per year throughout the shark's life.
It forms before birth and is never replaced, so it preserves the chemistry of the year the shark was born.
It is rebuilt continuously out of the material in whatever the shark has lately eaten.
It does not begin to form until the shark is roughly 150 years old.

questions.passage: A philologist argues that the anonymous chronicle was composed not in the monastery whose library held it but several hundred kilometers to the south.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the philologist's argument?
options: The parchment on which the chronicle is written was manufactured in the monastery's own workshop.
The chronicle describes a number of events that took place in the region surrounding the monastery.
The chronicle was catalogued in the monastery's library within a decade of its composition.
The chronicle's spellings of a dozen common words match the southern scribal convention exactly and never once follow the northern convention used in every other manuscript the monastery produced.

The subway stations proved more expensive to build than the transit authority had projected.
Some of the new stations were built in neighborhoods that already had frequent bus service.
Incomes also rose, though more slowly, in neighborhoods that received no subway station.

questions.passage: A museum found that visitors spent, on average, four seconds looking at each painting in its main gallery. When the wall labels were removed—the paintings themselves left otherwise untouched—average viewing time rose to eleven seconds. When the labels were restored but relocated to a booklet handed out at the entrance, viewing time settled at nine seconds. Since the paintings never changed, the results suggest that the original wall labels had been ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: drawing visitors' attention away from the paintings rather than merely adding information about them.
printed too small for most visitors in the gallery to read them comfortably.
supplying information that visitors found uninteresting or irrelevant to the works.
the only reason that most visitors entered the main gallery in the first place.

questions.passage: In a long-running study, employees offered a modest cash bonus for perfect attendance took fewer sick days in the first year than employees offered nothing at all. By the third year, however, the bonus group was taking more sick days than the group that had never been offered anything—and when the bonus was discontinued, their absences rose higher still. The pattern suggests that, over time, the bonus had ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: displaced whatever reason employees previously had for showing up with one that disappeared when the payment did.
grown too small to be worth the effort of earning it, although it was never actually reduced.
caused the employees who received it to fall ill more frequently than they had before.
been offered to a group of employees who happened to be unusually prone to illness.

  • Two hospitals introduced electronic records systems in 2022.

questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the difference in how long the two installations took. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Hospital V's system cost $12 million, while Hospital W's cost $9 million.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • “Shifting baseline syndrome” is when each generation treats the conditions of its own youth as normal.
  • Fishers in the 1950s considered a 3-meter fish an ordinary catch.
  • Fishers in the 1980s considered a 1-meter fish an ordinary catch.
  • Fishers today consider a 40-centimeter fish an ordinary catch.
  • Each generation measures decline only against what it personally remembers.
questions.question: The student wants to explain shifting baseline syndrome to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Fishers working today consider a fish of 40 centimeters to be an ordinary catch.
Each generation measures decline only against the conditions it personally remembers.

Shifting baseline syndrome is the habit of treating whatever you grew up with as normal—so fishers in the 1950s thought a 3-meter fish ordinary, those in the 1980s a 1-meter fish, and those today a 40-centimeter one, each measuring decline only against what they personally remember.
Shifting baseline syndrome is when each generation treats the conditions of its own youth as normal.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The researcher Iva Solt hypothesized that, among languages, those with more speakers tend to borrow a larger share of their vocabulary from other languages.
  • Language M: 800,000 speakers; 6% of its vocabulary borrowed.
  • Language N: 90 million speakers; 41% borrowed.
  • Language O: 7 million speakers; 19% borrowed.
questions.question: The student wants to use the data to support Solt's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The language with the most speakers, N (90 million), borrowed the largest share of its vocabulary (41%), while the language with the fewest, M (800,000), borrowed the smallest (6%).
Language O has 7 million speakers and has borrowed 19% of its vocabulary.
All three of the languages have borrowed at least some vocabulary from other languages.
Language N has more speakers than both Language M and Language O.
